title: Managing Six IAs Without Losing Your Weekends
summary: A practical September-November plan for managing six IAs, meeting school deadlines, protecting revision time, and keeping most weekends free in DP2.
body_markdown:
Managing six IAs without losing weekends requires one deadline map, a weekday production routine, and strict limits on how many assessments are active at once. During the **IB DP2 fall term** , move one high-risk IA forward, maintain one or two others, and park the rest at documented checkpoints.


This will not make September-November effortless. It will stop every subject from feeling urgent simultaneously and help preserve at least one substantial period of weekend rest.


### Clarify what “six IAs” means


The IB uses both internal and external assessment. Internally assessed work can include investigations, oral work, fieldwork, laboratory work, and artistic performance, so not every subject produces a conventional written report.


Your subjects may therefore create six different **coursework streams** , each with distinct criteria, feedback arrangements, and weightings. Consult the current subject information supplied by your teachers rather than applying one universal IA template.


The IB communicates official submission dates to schools, while schools set earlier student-facing deadlines for marking, authentication, standardization, and submission. Plan around the date given by your coordinator, even if an unofficial website lists a later IB deadline.


### Build one control sheet in September


Create a spreadsheet containing every IA, oral, practical component, EE checkpoint, TOK deadline, mock exam, university application, and important personal commitment. Ask teachers to confirm missing or provisional dates.


For each assessment, record:


- **School deadline** and personal deadline
- Current stage, such as question, evidence, draft, feedback, or final edit
- Next physical action
- Estimated focused sessions remaining
- Teacher questions awaiting answers
- Main risk, such as unavailable data or an overbroad question


Set personal deadlines **3-5 school days** before school deadlines. This buffer covers illness, technical problems, clarification, and final checks. It is not extra time for unnecessary rewriting.


### Follow a September-November IA plan


Adapt this sequence to your school calendar, particularly if you attend a November-session school or completed some components during DP1.


Period Main objective Measurable outputs


September Remove uncertainty and feasibility problems Confirmed dates, approved questions, criterion maps, evidence plans


October Produce evidence and substantial drafts Usable data, organized sources, calculations, figures, analysis


November Complete feedback cycles and submissions Full drafts, criterion-based revisions, references, technical checks


### September: eliminate uncertainty


Do not begin by perfecting introductions. Confirm that each research question is focused, the evidence is obtainable, and the proposed method can answer the question.


Create a one-page criterion map for every IA. Under each criterion, note what evidence the work needs and where it will appear. Use[RevisionDojo’s IA guides](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ia-guides) and your school’s current materials to understand unfamiliar requirements, but confirm important decisions with your teacher.


### October: prioritize evidence and analysis


Produce material that cannot be created safely at the last minute, including experimental data, calculations, selected passages, business documents, geographical evidence, or mathematical exploration. Drafting without adequate evidence often produces polished paragraphs that later need replacing.


End each session by recording a specific next action. “Calculate uncertainties for Table 2” is actionable; “continue Chemistry IA” is not.


### November: revise by criterion


Once a full draft exists, translate each permitted teacher comment into a criterion, weakness, and response. For example, “evaluation needs depth” could become: identify the two most significant limitations, explain how each affects the conclusion, and propose feasible improvements.


[RevisionDojo’s Coursework Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader) can offer a provisional rubric-based second opinion. It is not an official mark and should not replace teacher guidance.


### Keep only one IA in deep-work mode


Trying to advance six IAs equally fragments attention. Assign each assessment one of three statuses:


Status Meaning Weekly treatment


Deep work Closest, riskiest, or dependent on sustained reasoning Two or three 60-90 minute blocks


Maintenance Stable but requiring a limited task One 30-45 minute block


Holding No immediate action required Five-minute status check


Move an IA into deep-work mode when its deadline approaches, its method is uncertain, or it depends on laboratory access, participants, specialist sources, or teacher approval. Keep no more than one there unless two fixed deadlines genuinely collide.


This prevents the inefficient habit of opening all six documents every evening. Progress comes from completed outputs, not repeated contact with files.


### Design a week that protects the weekend


Place most IA production between Monday and Thursday. Use Friday for administration and retain one controlled weekend buffer rather than surrendering both days.


Day Suggested IA work


Monday 60-75 minutes on the deep-work IA


Tuesday 45-60 minutes on evidence or calculations


Wednesday 30-45 minutes on a maintenance IA


Thursday 60-75 minutes on analysis or revision


Friday 20-30 minutes for citations, files, and next actions


Saturday Optional 90-minute buffer before lunch


Sunday 15-minute weekly reset, otherwise protected


Leave Saturday empty unless a planned task slipped or a deadline is close. If the buffer is required every week, your tasks may be too large, your time estimates unrealistic, or your polishing excessive.


### Keep exam preparation active


IAs should not consume all subject study. Reserve three or four short weekly sessions for retrieval practice and exam-style questions, even during coursework-heavy periods.


Use[RevisionDojo’s IB resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib) to locate subject material, then combine Study Notes with targeted Questionbank practice. A focused 25-minute question set is generally more useful than passively reorganizing notes for an hour.[Coursework exemplars](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars) can clarify structure, but analyze them rather than copying wording, questions, or methods.


### Apply a stopping rule


Perfectionism consumes weekends because an IA never feels finished. Before each session, define a stopping point, such as completing one graph, revising one criterion, or checking five references.


Prioritize work in this order:


1. Missing evidence or analysis
2. Incorrect reasoning or methodology
3. Weak links to the research question
4. Criterion-specific revisions
5. Citations, labels, and technical compliance
6. Cosmetic wording changes


A rewritten introduction should never displace missing analysis. The[RevisionDojo IA success guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-internal-assessment-a-complete-guide-to-success-in-the-diploma-programme) explains question focus, feasibility, evidence, and feedback cycles in more detail.


### Avoid mistakes that consume weekends


Do not wait for a large free period because DP2 rarely provides one. Schedule small, observable deliverables during ordinary weekdays.


Common mistakes include treating all IAs as equally urgent, collecting more evidence before analyzing existing material, ignoring laboratory or participant availability, rewriting everything after feedback, and postponing exam revision until coursework is finished.


Do not use Jojo AI or another AI system to produce submission-ready analysis presented as your own. It can clarify terminology, explain feedback, or help formulate questions, but you must complete the assessed reasoning. The IB requires submitted work to be authentic, and its academic integrity policy addresses AI-produced material and acknowledgment.


### Recover when the plan slips


If you fall behind, do not immediately sacrifice the whole weekend. Identify what must be submitted, what can be reduced in scope, and what depends on another person.


Contact the relevant teacher early with a precise update: what is complete, what is blocking progress, and what you will produce next. Then reduce the week to three outcomes: one urgent deliverable, one important IA milestone, and one short exam-practice session.


### Conclusion


Managing six IAs without losing weekends is mainly a sequencing problem. Use your school’s deadlines, keep one IA in deep-work mode, define visible outputs, and reserve a small buffer instead of surrendering both weekend days.


RevisionDojo can support this system through IA Guides, coursework exemplars, Jojo AI explanations, and rubric-based Coursework Grader feedback. Use Study Notes and the Questionbank alongside these tools so coursework does not displace exam preparation.
